# Edge cases in the practice event log

## E1 - clock skew produces a negative lead time

- What the log contains: The practice event log contains 3 commit-deployment pairs where the commit timestamp occurs after the deployment timestamp due to clock skew between build servers.
- What a default definition would have done: A naive metric engine would calculate negative lead time durations or discard these commits from lead time calculations entirely.
- Why the rule is defensible: Clamping negative lead times to zero seconds preserves delivery tracking without skewing the median metric with impossible negative durations.

## E2 - a revert of a revert

- What the log contains: The practice event log contains 2 revert commits that target previous revert commits, forming a multi-step revert chain in repository history.
- What a default definition would have done: A standard parser would treat each revert commit as an independent change, artificially inflating change counts and altering lead times.
- Why the rule is defensible: Resolving revert chains transitively back to the original change ID reflects the actual net work delivered rather than administrative history.

## E3 - a hotfix that never touched `main`

- What the log contains: The log contains 4 distinct commit SHAs delivered directly to production from hotfix branches without ever being merged into main.
- What a default definition would have done: A standard pipeline parser filtering strictly on the main branch would completely ignore these production hotfix commits.
- Why the rule is defensible: Production deployments deliver code regardless of branch name, so all production-reaching commits must contribute to delivery lead time.

## E4 - a deployment with zero linked commits

- What the log contains: The event log includes 4 production deployments whose commits list is entirely empty, representing operational re-deployments or infrastructure updates.
- What a default definition would have done: A default metric pipeline might crash or fail when trying to associate lead time pairs with empty commit lists.
- Why the rule is defensible: Operational deployments still consume release capacity and risk failure, so they must count in frequency and fail rate while omitting lead time pairs.

## E5 - a deployment that failed and never recovered

- What the log contains: The log contains 1 failed production deployment whose covering incident was opened but never resolved within the observation log window.
- What a default definition would have done: A naive MTTR calculation might impute fake recovery durations or exclude open failures from instability calculations.
- Why the rule is defensible: Excluding unrecovered failures from recovery duration medians while counting them in open failure metrics accurately reports ongoing system risk.

## E6 - overlapping incidents

- What the log contains: The event log contains 11 pairs of distinct incidents whose open-to-resolution intervals overlap in time during system recovery periods.
- What a default definition would have done: A default incident tracker would merge overlapping incidents or double-count duration intervals when calculating MTTR.
- Why the rule is defensible: Recovery duration must be evaluated per failed deployment rather than per incident, ensuring independent MTTR measurements.

## Gaming demonstration

We demonstrated Goodhart's law by gaming deployment_frequency_per_day using rule R-11. We added 20 automated, empty production deployments during the window, which increased deployment frequency from 2.0 to 3.05 per day (+52.5% improvement). At the same time, we delayed actual base deployments carrying real feature changes, which degraded true change lead time from 149.8 hours to 421.5 hours (>280% worse delivery). In a real team, rewarding raw deployment frequency encourages engineering management to automate empty release triggers, creating an illusion of high velocity while delaying user value.
